mcqs.question: A hash map offers O(1) average lookup versus a small sorted array's O(log n) binary search. For a collection of 8 items, why might the array still win in practice?
options: The array wins because Big-O comparisons are only valid for collections over a certain size
The array wins because hashing is mathematically undefined for small n
The array wins because binary search is technically O(1) for n under 10

At n=8 the whole array fits in one or two cache lines and a linear or binary scan avoids the hash computation and pointer indirection entirely — the crossover to the hash map's advantage sits well above 8
mcqs.explanation: Big-O drops constant factors and only applies past a crossover point; at n=8 both structures fit in cache, but the array avoids hashing and pointer chasing altogether, so its lower constant factor wins below the crossover. Big-O is still valid at any n — it just isn't the thing that decides the winner this far below the threshold.

mcqs.question: A hot path needs to frequently answer 'give me every record with a timestamp between X and Y.' Which data structure is the right default, and why?
options: A hash map keyed by timestamp, since hash maps give O(1) lookups
A sorted structure (sorted array or balanced tree), since range queries need ordering that a hash map cannot provide without a full scan
A Bloom filter, since it is the most space-efficient structure available
Any structure works equally well since Big-O for lookups is the only relevant factor
mcqs.explanation: A hash map is excellent for exact-key lookups but has no concept of order, so a range query against one requires scanning every entry. A sorted array or balanced tree preserves order, letting a range query touch only the relevant contiguous span.

mcqs.question: A hot loop sums the `x` field across a million `{x, y, z, color}` structs. Switching from array-of-structs to struct-of-arrays layout makes the loop several times faster with no algorithmic change. Why?
options: Struct-of-arrays layout has a better asymptotic complexity than array-of-structs
The compiler always parallelizes struct-of-arrays code automatically across CPU cores
In array-of-structs, each cache line fetched contains y, z, and color that the loop never uses, wasting most of the memory bandwidth pulled in; struct-of-arrays fetches only the field actually read
Struct-of-arrays uses less total memory than array-of-structs for the same data
mcqs.explanation: Both layouts store the identical amount of data and both loops are Θ(n) — the speedup is purely from cache utilization: AoS wastes most of each fetched cache line on unused fields, while SoA makes every fetched byte useful, which is why a loop touching only one field runs faster with no algorithm change at all.

mcqs.question: A hot path allocates a fresh buffer on every call, thousands of times per second. What is the main risk of switching to a shared object pool instead?
options: Pooling introduces checkout/return discipline and a use-after-return bug class, and carries a fixed memory footprint even when idle — worth it only on a genuinely hot, measured path
Pooled objects are always slower than freshly allocated ones because they must be cleared before reuse
Object pools cannot be implemented in garbage-collected languages
Pooling only helps single-threaded code and actively hurts concurrent workloads
mcqs.explanation: Pooling trades allocator/GC overhead for real added complexity — a checkout/return protocol and the risk of using an object after it's returned to the pool — plus memory held even when unused. That trade-off is worth making on a measured hot path, not applied blanket-wide as premature optimization.

mcqs.question: Binary heaps are used for Dijkstra's algorithm far more often than Fibonacci heaps, even though Fibonacci heaps have better amortized asymptotic bounds. Why?
options: Fibonacci heaps are asymptotically worse than binary heaps in the worst case
Binary heaps' constant factors and simpler implementation outweigh Fibonacci heaps' asymptotic advantage at the sizes most real graphs actually run at
Fibonacci heaps cannot be implemented correctly in most programming languages
Binary heaps are the only heap variant that supports decrease-key operations
mcqs.explanation: Fibonacci heaps do have better amortized bounds, but their pointer-heavy structure and bookkeeping overhead mean the asymptotic win rarely materializes at practical graph sizes — the crossover point where they'd actually pay off sits far above what most real workloads need.

mcqs.question: A team replaces a linear scan over a 15-item list with a hash map lookup expecting a speedup, but the hot path gets measurably slower. What should have caught this before it shipped?
options: Nothing — this outcome is unpredictable and can only be discovered in production
Choosing a different hash function would have resolved the regression
Benchmarking the swap under realistic conditions before shipping, rather than trusting that a better asymptotic bound implies a real win at n=15
Reviewing the code for syntax errors, since a working hash map should always outperform a linear scan
mcqs.explanation: At n=15 the crossover point favoring the hash map likely hasn't been reached — the linear scan's lower constant factor wins. A benchmark under the actual workload, per Benchmarking Methodology, would have caught this before the regression shipped; asymptotic reasoning alone predicted the wrong outcome.
